tracks.name: Data Structures & Algorithms
tracks.desc: Arrays, strings, complexity, stacks, queues, linked lists, searching, sorting, recursion and trees — the exact toolkit technical interviews test, every one runnable in your browser.
outcomes: Solve array/string problems with two pointers
Implement stacks, queues, linked lists and trees
Search, sort and recurse with confidence

lessons.title: Arrays and strings: the two-pointer toolkit
lessons.content:
An array is just a list with positions

In Python the array you will use every day is the list. Every item has an index starting at 0. Almost every coding interview starts here: scanning a list, comparing items, moving pointers.

nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
nums[0]      # 4      first
nums[-1]     # 42     last
len(nums)    # 6
nums[1:3]    # [8, 15]  a slice

The two-pointer idea

Many problems are solved by two indices moving toward each other or together. Reversing, checking a palindrome, or finding a pair that sums to a target all use it.

i, j = 0, len(nums)-1
while i < j:
    # look at nums[i] and nums[j], then move a pointer
    i += 1
    j -= 1

Scanning to find something

biggest = nums[0]
for x in nums:
    if x > biggest:
        biggest = x
print(biggest)   # 42

exercises.q: Print the first and last item of the list, on two lines.
exercises.hint: nums[0] and nums[-1].
exercises.solution:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
print(nums[0])
print(nums[-1])

exercises.q: Find and print the largest number by scanning the list (don't use max).
exercises.starter:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
biggest = nums[0]
# loop and compare
exercises.hint: Loop, keep the biggest seen so far.
exercises.solution:
nums=[4,8,15,16,23,42]
b=nums[0]
for x in nums:
    if x>b: b=x
print(b)

exercises.q: Reverse the list using two pointers (not .reverse or [::-1]) and print it.
exercises.starter:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
i, j = 0, len(nums)-1
# swap ends, move inward
print(nums)
exercises.hint: Swap nums[i] and nums[j], then i+=1, j-=1, while i<j.
exercises.solution:
nums=[1,2,3,4,5]
i,j=0,len(nums)-1
while i<j:
    nums[i],nums[j]=nums[j],nums[i]
    i+=1; j-=1
print(nums)

exercises.q: Check if racecar is a palindrome with two pointers. Print True or False.
exercises.hint: Compare s[i] and s[j] moving inward; if any differ it's not a palindrome.
exercises.solution:
s='racecar'
i,j=0,len(s)-1
ok=True
while i<j:
    if s[i]!=s[j]: ok=False
    i+=1; j-=1
print(ok)

exercises.q: Two numbers in the list add up to 24. Print them (smaller first) on one line, space separated.
exercises.starter:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
# find a pair summing to 24
exercises.hint: Two loops; find i<j with nums[i]+nums[j]==24. That pair is 8 and 16.

lessons.title: Big-O: how to talk about speed
lessons.content:
Big-O counts the work as input grows

Big-O is not about seconds — it is about how the number of steps grows when the input gets bigger. Interviewers ask it constantly.

  • O(1) — constant. Reading nums[5] takes the same time no matter how big the list is.
  • O(n) — linear. One loop over n items. Doubling the list doubles the work.
  • O(n²) — quadratic. A loop inside a loop. 10 items = 100 steps, 100 items = 10,000.
  • O(log n) — logarithmic. Halving the problem each step (binary search).
# O(n): one pass
for x in nums:
    total += x

# O(n^2): nested pass — every pair
for i in range(len(nums)):
    for j in range(len(nums)):
        ...
Rule of thumb: count the deepest nesting of loops over the input. One loop = O(n). Two nested = O(n²).

exercises.q: Count how many steps a single loop over 5 items does. Print the count.
exercises.starter:
nums = [1,2,3,4,5]
steps = 0
# add 1 to steps each iteration
exercises.hint: steps += 1 inside a single for loop.
exercises.solution:
nums=[1,2,3,4,5]
steps=0
for x in nums:
    steps+=1
print(steps)

exercises.q: A nested loop over 5 items is O(n²). Print how many steps it does (5×5).
exercises.hint: steps += 1 in the inner loop; 5*5 = 25.

exercises.q: Binary search halves the range each step. Starting from 1000 items, print how many halvings until you reach 1 (count while dividing by 2). It is 9.
exercises.starter:
n = 1000
count = 0
# while n>1: halve it, count
exercises.hint: n = n//2 each loop; count the loops. ~9-10.
exercises.solution:
n=1000
count=0
while n>1:
    n=n//2
    count+=1
print(count)

exercises.q: Print the Big-O of reading one item by index, like nums[3]. (Print exactly: O(1))
exercises.starter: # what is the complexity of nums[3]?
exercises.hint: Indexing is constant time.
exercises.solution: print('O(1)')

lessons.title: Stacks and queues
lessons.content:
A stack is last-in, first-out (LIFO)

Think of a stack of plates: you add to the top and remove from the top. In Python a list is a ready-made stack: append to push, pop to pop.

stack = []
stack.append(1)   # push
stack.append(2)
stack.pop()       # 2  (last in, first out)

Stacks power undo buttons, the back button, and checking balanced brackets.

A queue is first-in, first-out (FIFO)

Like a line at a shop: first to arrive is first served. Use append to enqueue and pop(0) to dequeue (or collections.deque for speed).

queue = []
queue.append('a')  # enqueue
queue.append('b')
queue.pop(0)       # 'a'  (first in, first out)

exercises.q: Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop once and print what comes off.
exercises.hint: append three times, then pop() returns 3.

exercises.q: Enqueue 'a','b','c' into a queue, then dequeue once and print what comes off.
exercises.hint: append three, then pop(0) returns 'a'.

exercises.q: Use a stack to check if ( ( ) ) is balanced. Print True or False.
exercises.starter:
s = '(())'
stack = []
# push on '(', pop on ')'
exercises.hint: For '(' push; for ')' pop. Balanced if stack empties and never pops empty.

exercises.q: Check if ( ) ) is balanced (it is not). Print True or False.
exercises.hint: The extra ')' pops an empty stack → not balanced.

lessons.title: Linked lists
lessons.content:
A linked list is nodes joined by arrows

Instead of one block of memory like an array, a linked list is separate nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. Insertion is cheap; random access is not.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

a = Node(1)
b = Node(2)
a.next = b        # 1 -> 2

Walking the list

current = head
while current is not None:
    print(current.value)
    current = current.next
The classic interview task is reversing a linked list: flip every next pointer to face backwards, tracking previous, current and the next node so you don't lose the rest.

exercises.q: Build the chain 10 -> 20 -> 30 with Node objects and print each value on its own line by walking it.
exercises.hint: Set a.next=b, b.next=c. Then while current: print, move to .next.

exercises.q: Count how many nodes are in the chain 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8 by walking it. Print the count.
exercises.hint: Walk with a counter until current is None.

exercises.q: Reverse the chain 1 -> 2 -> 3 and print the values from the new head. Should print 3,2,1.
exercises.hint: prev=None; cur=head; while cur: nxt=cur.next; cur.next=prev; prev=cur; cur=nxt. New head is prev.

lessons.title: Searching and sorting
lessons.content:
Linear vs binary search

Linear search checks each item — O(n). Binary search works only on a sorted list and halves the range each step — O(log n).

# binary search for target in a sorted list
lo, hi = 0, len(a)-1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo+hi)//2
    if a[mid] == target: found
    elif a[mid] < target: lo = mid+1
    else: hi = mid-1

Sorting

You should understand one simple sort (bubble/insertion, both O(n²)) and know that Python's built-in sorted() is O(n log n) and is what you use in real life.

bubble idea: repeatedly swap neighbours that are out of order
print(sorted([3,1,2]))   # [1, 2, 3]

exercises.q: Binary search for 23 in the sorted list. Print the index it is found at.
exercises.hint: Compute mid=(lo+hi)//2, compare, move lo or hi. 23 is at index 4.
exercises.solution:
a=[4,8,15,16,23,42]
target=23
lo,hi=0,len(a)-1
while lo<=hi:
    mid=(lo+hi)//2
    if a[mid]==target:
        print(mid); break
    elif a[mid]<target: lo=mid+1
    else: hi=mid-1

exercises.q: Sort [5, 2, 9, 1, 7] using Python's sorted() and print the result.
exercises.hint: print(sorted(a)).
exercises.solution:
a=[5,2,9,1,7]
print(sorted(a))

exercises.q: Bubble sort [3, 1, 2] by hand (nested loop, swap neighbours) and print it sorted.
exercises.starter:
a = [3, 1, 2]
# nested loop, swap a[j],a[j+1] if out of order
exercises.hint: For each pass, swap neighbours that are out of order.

exercises.q: Linear-search for 15 and print its index (scan each item).
exercises.hint: Loop with enumerate; print the index when found. 15 is at index 2.

lessons.title: Recursion and trees
lessons.content:
Recursion: a function that calls itself

Every recursion needs a base case (when to stop) and a recursive case (a smaller version of the same problem).

def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:          # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n-1)   # smaller problem

Trees are recursive by nature

A binary tree node has a value and up to two children (left, right). Because each child is itself a tree, tree problems are naturally recursive.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.value = v
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def total(node):
    if node is None: return 0
    return node.value + total(node.left) + total(node.right)

exercises.q: Write factorial with recursion and print factorial(5).
exercises.starter:
def factorial(n):
    # base case then recursive case
    pass
print(factorial(5))
exercises.hint: if n<=1 return 1 else n*factorial(n-1). 5! = 120.

exercises.q: Sum 1+2+...+10 using recursion. Print the total.
exercises.starter:
def s(n):
    # base case n==0 -> 0
    pass
print(s(10))
exercises.hint: if n==0 return 0 else n+s(n-1). = 55.

exercises.q: Build a small tree (root 1, left 2, right 3) and print the sum of all values using recursion.
exercises.hint: total(node)=0 if None else value+total(left)+total(right). = 6.

tracks.name: Aptitude & Reasoning
tracks.desc: The quantitative and logical reasoning that fills the first round of most graduate hiring tests — percentages, ratios, profit/loss, speed and work, number series, and word puzzles you solve by computing.
outcomes: Do percentage, ratio and average problems fast
Handle profit/loss, interest, speed and work
Turn word puzzles into quick programs

lessons.title: Percentages, ratios and averages
lessons.content:
Percentages

"x percent" means x per 100. To take p% of a number: number * p / 100.

25% of 800  = 800 * 25/100 = 200
a 25% discount on 800 = 800 * (100-25)/100 = 600

Ratios

A ratio 2:3 splits a total into 2+3 = 5 parts. Each part = total / 5.

Averages

Average = sum of values / how many values.

In aptitude tests speed matters. Do the arithmetic in your head where you can, but here you'll compute it in Python to lock in the method.

exercises.q: A shirt costs 800. In a 25% off sale, what do you pay? Print the price.
exercises.solution:
price=800
print(int(price*(100-25)/100))

exercises.q: What is 15% of 240? Print it.
Split 1500 in the ratio 2:3. Print the two parts (smaller first) on two lines.
exercises.solution:
total=1500
p=total//5
print(2*p)
print(3*p)

exercises.q: The scores are 70, 85, 90, 95. Print the average.
exercises.solution:
scores=[70,85,90,95]
print(int(sum(scores)/len(scores)))

lessons.title: Profit, loss and interest
lessons.content:
Profit and loss

Profit = selling price − cost price. Profit percent is measured on the cost price: profit / cost * 100.

cost 500, sold 650  -> profit 150 -> 150/500*100 = 30%

Simple interest

interest = principal * rate * time / 100. Rate is percent per year, time in years.

2000 at 5% for 3 years -> 2000*5*3/100 = 300

exercises.q: Cost 500, sold for 650. Print the profit percent.
exercises.hint: (sell-cost)/cost*100 = 30.
exercises.solution:
cost=500; sell=650
print(int((sell-cost)/cost*100))

exercises.q: Simple interest on 2000 at 5% for 3 years. Print it.
exercises.solution:
p=2000; r=5; t=3
print(int(p*r*t/100))

exercises.q: An item marked 1200 is sold at a 10% loss. Print the selling price.
exercises.solution:
marked=1200
print(int(marked*(100-10)/100))

lessons.title: Speed, time and work
lessons.content:
Speed, time, distance

The one formula: distance = speed × time. Rearrange for what you need. Keep units consistent (km & hours, or m & seconds).

60 km/h for 2 h -> 120 km
120 km at 40 km/h -> 120/40 = 3 hours

Work

If someone does a job in n days, in one day they do 1/n of it. Two people together do 1/a + 1/b per day; time = 1 divided by that.

A: 10 days, B: 15 days -> per day 1/10+1/15 = 1/6 -> 6 days together

exercises.q: A car travels at 60 km/h for 2.5 hours. Print the distance (km).
exercises.hint: distance = speed*time = 150.
exercises.solution:
speed=60; time=2.5
print(int(speed*time))

exercises.q: How many hours to cover 240 km at 80 km/h? Print it.
exercises.hint: time = dist/speed = 3.
exercises.solution:
dist=240; speed=80
print(int(dist/speed))

exercises.q: A does a job in 10 days, B in 15 days. Print how many days together.
exercises.solution:
a=10; b=15
rate=1/a+1/b
print(int(round(1/rate)))

lessons.title: Numbers, series and patterns
lessons.content:
Number series

Find the rule connecting the terms: adding a constant, multiplying, squares, or differences that themselves form a pattern.

2, 4, 6, 8, ?     -> +2 each -> 10
3, 6, 12, 24, ?   -> ×2 each -> 48
1, 4, 9, 16, ?    -> squares -> 25

Divisibility, GCD, LCM, primes

  • GCD — biggest number dividing both. LCM — smallest number both divide.
  • A prime has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself.
import math
math.gcd(12, 18)   # 6

exercises.q: Continue the series 3, 6, 12, 24, ... Print the next term.
exercises.solution: print(24*2)

exercises.q: Print the next term of 1, 4, 9, 16, ... (they are squares).
exercises.solution: print(5**2)

exercises.q: Print the GCD of 24 and 36.
exercises.solution:
import math
print(math.gcd(24,36))

exercises.q: Print all prime numbers below 10, one per line.
exercises.hint: A number is prime if no number from 2..n-1 divides it.

lessons.title: Logical reasoning you can compute
lessons.content:
Turn word puzzles into small programs

Many logical-reasoning questions become easy when you let the computer try every possibility. This is exactly how you'd verify your reasoning in an interview too.

# "A number, doubled and increased by 3, gives 17. What is it?"
for n in range(1, 100):
    if 2*n + 3 == 17:
        print(n)   # 7

Counting and arrangements

How many 2-digit numbers can be made from digits 1,2,3 with no repeat? Try them all and count.

count = 0
for a in [1,2,3]:
    for b in [1,2,3]:
        if a != b:
            count += 1
print(count)   # 6

exercises.q: A number doubled and increased by 3 gives 17. Find it by trying values. Print it.
exercises.hint: Loop and test 2*n+3==17. Answer 7.

exercises.q: How many two-digit numbers can be formed from 1,2,3 with no repeated digit? Print the count.
exercises.starter:
count = 0
# try all a,b with a!=b
exercises.hint: Nested loop over [1,2,3], count when a!=b. Answer 6.

exercises.q: Three consecutive numbers add up to 72. Print the middle one.
exercises.hint: The middle is n+1. Sum is 3n+3=72 → n=23, middle 24.
